newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Japanese big business hails APEC free trade vows.
newsitem.headline: Japanese big business hails APEC free trade vows.

text.p: Japanese big business gave the loudest cheer in Asia on Monday for "momentous" efforts made by APEC leaders towards ensuring free trade and stability in the region.
The Keidanren business group, which includes all Japan's biggest corporations, welcomed the declaration made in the Philippines after the summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.

Leaders of the 18-member APEC, which includes industrial powerhouse Japan, earlier on Monday promised to take concrete steps to meet the goal of setting up the world's biggest free trade zone by 2020.
The group also pledged to press for a global accord on free trade in information technology products through the World Trade Organisation.

"The joint meeting held by the leaders of APEC is a momentous step in the process of securing stability and prosperity in the Pacific," Keidanren said in a statement. "The signing of the Manila Action Plan is a commendable achievement, as it signifies the beginning phase of trade and investment liberalisation and harmonisation."

The Manila Action Plan details the steps each APEC summit has taken to lower trade barriers and outlines what they plan to do in future. It also spells out ways to speed up the movement of both goods and people by streamlining customs and immigration rules.
Taiwan media hailed the free trade zone commitment, but said the declaration should be developed as an international agreement.
"Unfortunately APEC still keeps its structure as a forum which does not have the nature of an international agreement," the China Times newspaper said in its editorial.

David Lee, spokesman for Taiwan's APEC delegation, said he did not expect a change in U.S. policy towards Taiwan because of the summits in Washington and Beijing promised by presidents Bill Clinton and Jiang Zemin.

"The United States will not sacrifice Taiwan's interests for the development of relations with communist China," Lee said in Manila. China has considered Taiwan a renegade province since the two countries were separated by civil war in 1949.
Economists in the region were not particularly impressed by APEC's free trade promises.

"They were talking about the very distant future," said K.K. Chan, chief economist at Nomura Research Institute in Tokyo. He said there would be practical difficulties in implementing the plans until many of the poorer Asian economies had developed.

Liew Yin Sze, an economist with J.M. Sassoon in Singapore agreed. "The free trade issue is nothing new. Everybody seems to be working towards it, even without APEC. For example, the AFTA (Association of Southeast Asian Nations Free Trade Area) is already in place. This kind of thing is easy to say," he said of the plan to build a free trade zone by 2020. "It will be difficult to work out the details."

The APEC leaders acknowledged the diversity of an organisation that includes the United States, Japan and China alongside a minnow such as Papua New Guinea but stressed the importance of developing a sense of community.
The Independent newspaper in impoverished Bangladesh, which is not an APEC member, said the group, despite its diversity, had managed to take the world by surprise.

"The association of developed countries like the United States and Japan with APEC has proved to be mutually beneficial and helped in confidence building which in turn will help in putting the region on a solid economic foundation," it said.
